Prealgebra · Lesson 1.5

Division

Solve this lesson, free →All lessons

Subtraction turned out to be addition, since a−ba−b is just a+(−b)a+(−b), and the opposite of bb was the partner that made it work. That leaves the last operation, division. Here is a guess worth holding onto. If subtraction was another form of addition, division will be another form of multiplication, and it will need a partner of its own.

Problem
A blueprint app has one button that scales every length by 5, blowing a drawing up to five times its size. You tap it by accident. You need a second scaling that puts the drawing back exactly as it was, neither bigger nor smaller. Multiplying by 11 is the scaling that changes nothing, so what number must you scale by to undo the ×5×5?
Show a hint
  • What single number multiplies with 5 to give 1?
Show the full solution
Scaling up by 5 and back down acts like multiplying by 1, so you need the number that turns 5 into 1.5×15=15×51​=1The undo scales by 1551​​, the reciprocal of 5.
Problem
Here is a pattern worth predicting before you compute. Last chapter, the opposite of the opposite of a number brought you right back to the number, since two flips across zero return home. Now guess the reciprocal of a reciprocal, then test the guess. What is the reciprocal of 1661​?
Show a hint
  • The reciprocal of 1661​ is the number that multiplies with 1661​ to give 1.
  • Flip 1661​ over.
Show the full solution
Flip 1661​ and it becomes 6.16×6=161​×6=1So the reciprocal of 1661​ is 66​. Flipping twice returns the original, so the reciprocal of a reciprocal is the number itself.
Problem
One number has no reciprocal at all. Try to find the reciprocal of 00, the partner that would multiply with 0 to give 1. Hunt for it, and say what goes wrong.
Show the full solution
The reciprocal of 0 would have to turn 0 into 1, but 0×(any number)=00×(any number)=0, never 1. So 0 has no reciprocal, the only number without one.
Problem
Last chapter, exactly one number was its own opposite, the number 0, sitting right on its own mirror image. Now ask the matching question for reciprocals. How many numbers are their own reciprocal, equal to the number that multiplies with them to give 1? Test small cases and see what you find.
Show a hint
  • A number xx is its own reciprocal when x×x=1x×x=1.
  • Try 1. Then remember the sign rule and try −1−1.
Show the full solution
A number is its own reciprocal when it times itself gives 1. 1×1=11×1=1, and (−1)×(−1)=1(−1)×(−1)=1, so 1 and −1−1 both qualify. Nothing else does, since any number above 1 has a reciprocal below 1. That leaves exactly 22​ such numbers.
Key idea
Every number except 0 has a reciprocal, the number that multiplies with it to give 1. It is written 1bb1​, so b×1b=1b×b1​=1. The reciprocal does for multiplication what the opposite does for addition. To find a fraction’s reciprocal, flip it (ab→baba​→ab​), and flipping twice returns the original. A number and its reciprocal always share a sign, since their product is a positive 1.

With the reciprocal in hand, we can build division out of multiplication. First we check the new rule against a division you already know the answer to, then use it on a division that is awkward to do the old way.

Problem
A relay team of 44 runners splits a 1212 km course into equal legs. Plain division says each leg is 12÷4=312÷4=3 km, no surprise. Now compute it the new way instead. Take 1441​ of 12, that is 12×1412×41​. How long is each leg this way?
Show the full solution
Each runner covers one quarter of 12 km, found by multiplying.12×14=124=312×41​=412​=3​Dividing 12 by 4 and multiplying 12 by 1441​ are two names for one number.
Problem
Undo a ×6×6: compute 24÷6.24÷6.
Show a hint
  • Dividing by 6 undoes multiplying by 6.
Show the full solution
24÷6=424÷6=4​, since 4×6=244×6=24.
Problem
A jar holds 3 cups of flour. Your scoop holds 1441​ cup. How many full scoops fill the jar? In symbols, find 3÷14.3÷41​.
Show a hint
  • Dividing by 1441​ means multiplying by the reciprocal of 1441​.
  • The reciprocal of 1441​ is 4, so you are really computing 3×43×4.
Show the full solution
Turn the division into multiplication by the reciprocal of 1441​, which is 4.3÷14=3×4=123÷41​=3×4=12​The answer grew past 3 because we divided by a number below 1, whose reciprocal is bigger than 1.
Problem
How many halves fill 6? Find 6÷12.6÷21​.
Show a hint
  • Dividing by 1221​ is multiplying by 22.
Show the full solution
6÷12=6×2=126÷21​=6×2=12​, so twelve halves make six.
Key idea
Division is multiplication by the reciprocal. This gives a÷b=a×1ba÷b=a×b1​ (for b≠0b=0), which matches a−b=a+(−b)a−b=a+(−b). It is also why you cannot divide by 0, since that would mean multiplying by 0’s reciprocal, and 0 has none. Because 1bb1​ can be bigger than 1, dividing by a number between 0 and 1 makes the result larger, since dividing by 1441​ is multiplying by 4.
Problem
Over 66 equal stages of a dive, a submarine’s depth changed by a total of −240−240 m (a downward move counts as negative, as it did two lessons ago). The stages were identical, so what was the depth change per stage? Compute −240÷6.−240÷6.
Show a hint
  • Division is multiplication by the reciprocal, so this is −240×16−240×61​.
  • One negative factor flips the sign of the product, just as it did for multiplication.
Show the full solution
Rewrite the division as multiplication by 1661​. One negative factor keeps the result negative.−240÷6=−240×16=−40−240÷6=−240×61​=−40​Division uses the same sign rules as multiplication, because it is multiplication by the reciprocal.
Problem
Structure beats grinding, as always. Compute (16×21)÷(8×3)(16×21)÷(8×3) without doing the two multiplications first. Look for parts of the top that pair off neatly with parts of the bottom.
Show a hint
  • Dividing by 8×38×3 is multiplying by 18×1381​×31​, so pair the 16 with the 8 and the 21 with the 3.
  • 16÷8=216÷8=2 and 21÷3=721÷3=7.
Show the full solution

Pair each top factor with the bottom factor it cancels.

(16×21)×18×13=(16×18)×(21×13)=2×7=14(16×21)×81​×31​=(16×81​)×(21×31​)=2×7=14​

Grinding out 336÷24336÷24 gives 14 as well, but pairing first means you never build the big products.

Key idea
In a quotient of products, pair each top factor with a bottom factor it cancels with, and clear those pairs before you multiply anything. Each cancelled pair leaves a 1 behind, so you never build the big products at all.
Problem
Pair, do not grind: (25×18)÷(5×9).(25×18)÷(5×9).
Show a hint
  • Pair 25 with 5, and 18 with 9.
Show the full solution
Pair the factors. 25÷5=525÷5=5 and 18÷9=218÷9=2, so the value is 5×2=105×2=10​.
Problem
Sometimes the top and bottom share a factor so ugly you would dread computing it. Find (637×50)÷(637×10).(637×50)÷(637×10). The 637 is bait. Do not take it.
Show a hint
  • 637 sits on both the top and the bottom. What does 637×1637637×6371​ equal?
  • Whatever 637 is, it cancels to 1, leaving only 50÷1050÷10.
Show the full solution

The 637 on top meets a 16376371​ on the bottom, and that pair cancels to 1.

637×50×1637×110=1×(50÷10)=5637×50×6371​×101​=1×(50÷10)=5​

A factor sitting on both the top and the bottom always cancels to 1, however big it is, so you never multiply it out.

Problem
A signal runs through a pipeline that multiplies it by 1414, then by 2727, then by 1010. Three filters then divide it by 77, by 99, and by 55. By what single factor does the signal change overall? Compute (14×27×10)÷(7×9×5)(14×27×10)÷(7×9×5) by pairing, not by grinding.
Show a hint
  • Turn every division into multiplication by a reciprocal, then hunt for pairs.
  • 14 with 7, 27 with 9, 10 with 5. Each pair divides cleanly.
Show the full solution

Spread the three divisions out as reciprocals and pair each top factor with the bottom factor that cancels it.

(14÷7)×(27÷9)×(10÷5)=2×3×2=12(14÷7)×(27÷9)×(10÷5)=2×3×2=12​

The signal comes out 12 times bigger, and none of the six original multiplications had to be carried out.

Problem
Addition and multiplication let you reorder and regroup at will. Division is stricter, and it is worth catching in the act. First, is 12÷312÷3 the same as 3÷123÷12? Then settle a grouping question. Compute 24÷(4÷2)24÷(4÷2) and compare it to (24÷4)÷2(24÷4)÷2. Enter the value of 24÷(4÷2).24÷(4÷2).
Show a hint
  • Work inside the parentheses first. 4÷2=24÷2=2, so the left side is 24÷224÷2.
  • Compare with (24÷4)÷2=6÷2(24÷4)÷2=6÷2.
Show the full solution

Inside the parentheses, 4÷2=24÷2=2, so

24÷(4÷2)=24÷2=1224÷(4÷2)=24÷2=12​

Move the parentheses and you get (24÷4)÷2=6÷2=3(24÷4)÷2=6÷2=3, a different answer from the same three numbers. Order fails too, since 12÷3=412÷3=4 while 3÷12=143÷12=41​. Division flips only the number you divide by, so shuffling the numbers changes which one gets flipped.

Key idea
You cannot reorder or regroup a division, but the fix is the one that already worked for subtraction. Turn every ÷b÷b into ×1b×b1​ first, the same way every minus became “add the opposite.” Once the whole expression is one long product, you may reorder, regroup, and cancel it however you like.
Problem
Mind the signs. (−56×9)÷(7×(−3)).(−56×9)÷(7×(−3)).
Show a hint
  • Negative over negative is positive, then pair off.
Show the full solution
Two negatives make the result positive, and then (56÷7)×(9÷3)=8×3=24(56÷7)×(9÷3)=8×3=24​.
Problem
Put every tool in one place. Compute (−45×16)÷(−9×4)(−45×16)÷(−9×4) in your head. Mind the signs, convert the division, then pair off.
Show a hint
  • Two negative numbers are involved, so the result is positive. Now just handle the sizes.
  • Write it as 45×16×19×1445×16×91​×41​ and pair 45 with 9, then 16 with 4.
Show the full solution

One negative on top and one on the bottom make the result positive, so drop both signs and pair the factors.

45×16×19×14=(45÷9)×(16÷4)=5×4=2045×16×91​×41​=(45÷9)×(16÷4)=5×4=20​

Signs first, then division turned into multiplication, then pairs that cancel. Three lessons in one short computation.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Compute (9+18+27+36)÷(36+27+18+9).(9+18+27+36)÷(36+27+18+9).
Show the solution
The numbers above the line and below it are identical, only listed in reverse, so the two sums are equal. Any nonzero amount divided by itself is 11​, you never have to add a single thing.
Practice
Compute 5,600,000÷70,0005,600,000÷70,000 by cancelling, not by long division.
Show the solution
Strike four matching zeros from the top and the bottom, and 5,600,000÷70,0005,600,000÷70,000 becomes 560÷7=80560÷7=80​. Cancelling equal factors of 10 from top and bottom never changes a quotient.
Practice
Compute (317×317)÷317(317×317)÷317 without ever multiplying 317 by itself.
Show the solution
Dividing a product by one of its own factors simply hands back the other factor, so the answer is 317317​. Multiplying by a number and then dividing by it is a round trip straight back to the start.
Practice
A ribbon is 66 metres long. How many 1551​-metre bookmarks can you cut from it? Compute 6÷15.6÷51​.
Show the solution
Five fifths fit in every metre, so six metres give 6×5=306×5=30​ bookmarks. Dividing by 1551​ means multiplying by its reciprocal, 5, and the count grows past 6 because the piece you cut is tiny.
Practice
Compute 20÷25.20÷52​.
Show the solution
Flip the divisor and multiply. 20÷25=20×52=1002=5020÷52​=20×25​=2100​=50​.
Practice
What number is 4 less than the value of 48÷3448÷43​?
Show the solution
48÷34=48×43=6448÷43​=48×34​=64, and 64−4=6064−4=60​. Dividing by a number below 1 makes the result bigger, which catches almost everyone off guard the first time.
Practice
Compute (13×40×9)÷(9×13)(13×40×9)÷(9×13) by cancelling first.
Show the solution
The 9 and the 13 on top each meet a copy on the bottom and cancel to 1, leaving the lone 4040​. Neither big product was ever worth forming.
Practice
Compute (20×50×90)÷(2×5×9).(20×50×90)÷(2×5×9).
Show the solution
Pair and divide. 20÷2=1020÷2=10, 50÷5=1050÷5=10, and 90÷9=1090÷9=10, so the whole expression is 10×10×10=100010×10×10=1000​. Scaling every factor up by ten multiplies the quotient by ten, once for each factor.
Practice
Compute (4,000,000+36)÷4(4,000,000+36)÷4 by sharing the division across the sum.
Show the solution
Divide each piece on its own. 4,000,000÷4+36÷4=1,000,000+9=1,000,0094,000,000÷4+36÷4=1,000,000+9=1,000,009​. Splitting the dividend into friendly chunks beats one monstrous long division.
Practice
Compute (72+56+40+24)÷(9+7+5+3)(72+56+40+24)÷(9+7+5+3) by comparing the two sums.
Show the solution
Every top term is eight times its partner (72=8×972=8×9, 56=8×756=8×7, 40=8×540=8×5, 24=8×324=8×3), so the whole top is eight times the whole bottom. A quantity divided by one-eighth of itself is 88​, and not a single sum had to be worked out.
Practice
Compute 96÷12÷12÷13,96÷21​÷21​÷31​, working left to right.
Show the solution
Working left to right, 96÷12=19296÷21​=192, then 192÷12=384192÷21​=384, then 384÷13=1152384÷31​=1152​. Two doublings and a tripling multiply 96 by 2×2×3=122×2×3=12.
Practice
Compute (45×28)÷(35×18)(45×28)÷(35×18) without multiplying either product out.
Show the solution
Cancel in stages. 45 and 35 share 5, leaving 9 and 7, and 28 and 18 share 2, leaving 14 and 9. Now (9×14)÷(7×9)(9×14)÷(7×9), where the 9 cancels and 14÷7=214÷7=2, so the answer is 22​. Clearing shared factors first turns four awkward numbers into a single digit.
Practice
Watch what division does as the divisor shrinks. 12÷1=1212÷1=12, then 12÷12=2412÷21​=24, then 12÷14=4812÷41​=48, then 12÷1100=120012÷1001​=1200. The closer the divisor gets to 00, the larger the quotient grows, with no ceiling anywhere. That is the real reason you cannot divide by 00, since there is no single number the quotient would settle on, only values that grow without end.
